title: WITAWITADD - Slow Questing
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8r9S_xIzqLk

Back at work after a vacation's worth of daily videos, Daniel (@dungeondive) names the practice that keeps him gaming anyway: slow questing. Leave a game set up on the table and take a single turn whenever you pass it — a work break, a gap in the yard work — over days rather than an evening.

Not every game survives it. The test is upkeep: come back after six hours and you need to know instantly whose turn it is and what phase you're in. Runebound Second Edition passes perfectly: a full turn in five minutes, nothing to track. He's playing it with the Sands of Al-Kalim expansion, whose desert-survival focus on fatigue and water wears on him. The house rules that keep it brisk: item decks split into weapons, armour and a combined magic-item deck, each market seeded face-up on a d4 roll; levelling costs 2 XP plus one per level token already held, so early levels come cheap; one gold heals all wounds; and treasure lost on death attaches to the creature that killed you, to be won back.

The other slow quest is Fabled Lands, the 1996 Morris and Thompson gamebook series he came to late. He makes the case for it as a peak of the form: towns with tickboxes that advance in your absence, a house you can buy in Yellowport to store items you can't carry, codewords triggering bespoke events, and books linked geographically so sailing east means turning to Book Three.

----

Do you slow-quest — a game left standing for days, a turn at a time? Which games tolerate it, and which punish you the moment you walk away?
